why.correct: S colonies appear with untreated extract (46), protease-treated (44) and RNase-treated (49) extract, but not when DNA was destroyed (0). Only DNase removes the transforming activity, so DNA is the molecule required.
options: Correct: only the DNase treatment dropped S colonies to zero, matching the R-alone control.
Destroying protein left 44 S colonies, about the same as untreated extract, so protein is not required; RNase also left activity.
The extract was cell-free, and tube 5 had the same dead-cell material yet grew no S colonies; the change depends on DNA, not revival.
A capsule handed over would not be copied by dividing cells; colonies arise from many divisions, so the cells must have gained the ability to make capsules.

why.correct: Boiling denatures the DNase but leaves everything else in the preparation. Tube 6 kept its S colonies (45), so tube 5's result was due to active DNase digesting DNA, not to a contaminant or the added protein.
options: Correct: it is a control that keeps every ingredient of tube 5 except the enzyme's activity.
The DNase, not the extract, was boiled; and tube 6 grew 45 S colonies, so the DNA in the extract still worked.
Tube 1 is the R-alone control; tube 6 contains S extract and DNase.
Boiled DNase is not a candidate transforming agent; it is there so the only difference from tube 5 is whether the enzyme works.

why.correct: Total colonies = 2,950 + 46 = 2,996. S-type share = 46 ÷ 2,996 × 100 = 1.54%, which rounds to 1.5%. Transformation changes only a small fraction of the R cells.
Transformation is a heritable change: the DNA taken in becomes part of the cell's own genetic material and is copied before each division, so the descendants keep the S trait without more extract.
options: Correct: the gained DNA is passed on like the rest of the chromosome.
DNA is copied before division, so both daughter cells receive the gene; it is not split between them.
Once the DNA is part of the cell's genome, the trait does not depend on the extract still being present; this is the evidence that heredity changed.
Nothing removes the new DNA; S cells recovered from Griffith's mice stayed S when grown and injected again.

why.correct: If protein were the agent, removing it should remove the activity. Highly purified DNA, with protein below detection, keeps full activity per microgram, so protein is not needed.
options: Correct: activity tracks the DNA, not the protein.
44 against 46 is within the plate-to-plate spread, and in any case it would not separate DNA from protein as the cause.
This is Griffith's control showing the dead cells alone are harmless; it says nothing about which molecule transforms.
R colony counts measure the R cells that grew, not transformation, and the critic's leftover protein could still be present.

why.correct: After blending, 79% of the <sup>32</sup>P was in the cell pellet, but 82% of the <sup>35</sup>S was in the liquid with the shaken-off coats.
options: Correct: phosphorus-labeled DNA went in; sulfur-labeled protein stayed outside.
This reverses the table: <sup>35</sup>S was 18% in the pellet and 82% in the liquid.
The splits are 18/82 and 79/21, far from even.
Only 31% of the <sup>32</sup>P and under 1% of the <sup>35</sup>S were recovered in new phages.

why.correct: Two of the twenty amino acids carry sulfur, and DNA has none; every DNA nucleotide carries a phosphate, and phage protein has essentially none. So <sup>35</sup>S tracks protein and <sup>32</sup>P tracks DNA.
options: Correct: the labels distinguish the two candidate molecules.
A label marks the molecules that contain the element, not a location; that is why the element had to differ between DNA and protein.
The batches were labeled and run separately; the choice of elements was about which molecules carry them.
If both molecules carried both elements, neither label could tell DNA from protein.

why.correct: Without blending, 92% of the <sup>35</sup>S spun down with the cells, so attached coats pellet with them; blending removes most but not all. Protein that entered and acted would show up in new phages, but under 1% did.
options: Correct: incomplete removal of attached coats explains the pellet <sup>35</sup>S.
Protein that directed new phages would be found in them, but under 1% of the <sup>35</sup>S was recovered there.
DNA contains no sulfur, so <sup>35</sup>S cannot become part of DNA.
Broken cells would explain <sup>32</sup>P in the liquid, not <sup>35</sup>S in the pellet.

why.correct: A useful label must be in one candidate molecule and not the other. Every organic molecule contains carbon, so <sup>14</sup>C would be found in both the pellet and the liquid whatever entered the cell.
options: Correct: a label common to both molecules cannot separate them.
Bacteria build their molecules from the carbon in their food, so phages grown in them would be labeled; the problem is that every molecule would be.
Nothing suggests radioactive carbon would kill the cells; the design flaw is that it marks both molecules.
Even if some carbon were reused later, the label would start in both molecules, so it could not tell them apart.

why.correct: Almost a third of the parent's <sup>32</sup>P was passed on to the offspring phages, but under 1% of its <sup>35</sup>S. What passes from parent to offspring is DNA, as expected of hereditary material.
options: Correct: the parental DNA appears in the next generation.
Under 1% of the coat label reached the new phages, so the old coat is not reused.
31% of the parental <sup>32</sup>P turned up in the new phages, so the DNA was not all destroyed.
Protein contains almost no phosphorus; the <sup>32</sup>P in the new phages is in their DNA.

why.correct: A (a purine) pairs with T (a pyrimidine), and G (a purine) pairs with C (a pyrimidine).
options: Correct: every rung combines a two-ring base and a one-ring base.
Two two-ring bases would be too long to fit between the backbones.
Two one-ring bases would be too short to reach each other and bond.
Phosphates are in the backbone; a base pair is two bases.

why.correct: A and G are both purines (two rings), C and T both pyrimidines (one ring). Purine–purine rungs would be long and pyrimidine–pyrimidine rungs short, so the helix would bulge and pinch instead of keeping a uniform width.
options: Correct: uniform width depends on every pair being one purine plus one pyrimidine.
The width would not stay the same, because the rungs would have two different lengths.
Strand direction is set by the backbone chemistry, which the question keeps the same.
A strand can have any mix of bases; pairing rules constrain the two strands together, so this does not follow.

why.correct: A bacterium has no nucleus. Its main DNA is one circular chromosome in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and many carry plasmids as well.
options: Correct: one circular chromosome, with no nuclear envelope around it.
Correct: plasmids are common, and their genes (for example for surviving a drug) can be useful.
Several linear chromosomes in a nucleus describe a eukaryote.
Histones and nucleosomes package eukaryotic DNA; bacteria fold their DNA with other proteins.
One chromosome carries thousands of genes; a cell does not hold one chromosome per gene.

why.correct: In heterochromatin the DNA is wound so tightly that the proteins that read genes mostly cannot bind. When that packing spreads into a neighboring gene, the gene is silenced in the cells where it spreads, with no change in sequence.
options: Correct: packing controls access, so the same gene can be on or off.
The stem says the sequence is unchanged, and a gene in pieces would not be fully restored in other cells.
Packing changes how accessible DNA is, not its base sequence; the stem rules out a sequence change.
Chromosomes stay in the nucleus; the gene moved along the chromosomes, not out of the nucleus.

why.correct: Each nucleotide's phosphate carries a negative charge, so DNA's outside is strongly negative. Positively charged side chains attract it, letting the DNA wrap tightly around the histone core.
options: Correct: opposite charges attract (ionic interactions).
The bases pair with each other inside the helix; histones contact the backbone on the outside.
Repulsion would push DNA away from histones, not wrap it around them.
The attraction is ionic and can loosen when charges change; histones do not bond covalently to the sugars.

why.correct: Only live R cells were injected alive, yet live S cells came out. R cells must have gained the S trait from the dead cells, and kept it as they multiplied.
options: Correct: live S cells appeared where only dead S cells had gone in.
This only shows that S is deadly and R is not; it is the starting point, not evidence of transfer.
This control shows the dead S cells alone are harmless, but nothing passes anywhere in it.
Sickness alone could mean the dead cells harmed the mice with help from R; recovering live S cells is what shows the R cells changed.

why.correct: Packing controls access. Opening the chromatin lets the proteins that read genes reach more DNA and shrinks the heterochromatin, but the amount of DNA and its sequence stay the same.

variables.name: Number of genes whose DNA the gene-reading proteins can reach
variables.why: Looser chromatin (more like euchromatin) exposes more DNA to the proteins that read genes.

variables.name: Total amount of DNA in the nucleus
variables.why: Loosening changes how the DNA is packed, not how much DNA there is.

variables.name: Share of the chromatin that is tightly packed heterochromatin
variables.why: The drug opens chromatin, so less of it stays in the tightly packed form.

variables.name: Base sequence of each gene
variables.why: Packing affects access to DNA, not the order of its bases.

why.correct: Each level folds the one before it: the helix wraps histones, nucleosomes coil into a fiber, the fiber folds into loops, and in mitosis the loops condense into the compact chromosome you can see under a light microscope.
If RNA by itself can start an infection that produces whole new viruses, coat and all, then the RNA carries the instructions; this was shown for tobacco mosaic virus in the 1950s.
options: Correct: the RNA alone is sufficient to make complete offspring viruses.
This describes what the particle contains, not which part carries the instructions.
More RNA in sick leaves could come from the plant's own response; it does not test which molecule is hereditary.
Being single-stranded says nothing about whether the molecule carries the hereditary instructions.

why.correct: In the conservative model the parent molecule stays whole (heavy) and the copy is entirely new (light), so generation 1 would show heavy and light bands. Tube B has a single intermediate band.
options: Correct: there is no heavy band and no light band in tube B.
The semiconservative model predicts exactly tube B's single intermediate band, so tube B fits it.
The dispersive model also predicts one intermediate band after one generation, so tube B cannot rule it out.
The conservative model predicts two bands, not an intermediate one, so tube B does rule it out.

why.correct: In the dispersive model every strand is a patchwork of old and new DNA. After two generations all molecules would be one quarter heavy (one band, between intermediate and light), and separated generation-1 strands would all be half heavy (one band). Tube C shows a fully light band, and tube D shows separate heavy and light strands.
options: Tube A is the starting DNA; every model starts with it.
One intermediate band after one generation is predicted by the dispersive model too.
Correct: a fully light band at generation 2 means some molecules have no old DNA at all, which dispersal cannot produce.
Correct: generation-1 molecules contain one whole heavy strand and one whole light strand, not two half-heavy strands.
Tube E is a reference that marks the heavy and light positions; it tests no model.

why.correct: Each original molecule gives 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 molecules after four generations. Its two heavy strands survive intact, one in each of 2 hybrid molecules; the other 14 are fully light. 2 ÷ 16 = 12.5%.
Generation 2 has 4 molecules per original: 2 hybrid (one heavy and one light strand each) and 2 fully light. That is 8 strands: 2 heavy and 6 light, so a quarter heavy and three quarters light.
options: Correct: 2 heavy strands out of 8, the rest light.
Equal bands describe generation 1 (one heavy and one light strand per molecule), not generation 2.
Copying keeps each old strand whole, so no strand is half heavy; that would be the dispersive model.
This reverses the proportions; new strands are light, and they outnumber the two original heavy strands.

why.correct: After many generations, almost every nitrogen atom in the DNA is <sup>15</sup>N, so every molecule starts fully heavy. Any lighter DNA after the shift must then contain newly made strands.
options: Correct: the experiment needs every starting strand to be labeled.
Growth rate is not what the density method measures; the long growth is about labeling.
Heavy nitrogen changes density, not how easily the strands separate.
The cells kept dividing in <sup>15</sup>N; the point was to label all their DNA.

why.correct: The normal strain goes from 51% to 3% in two minutes, while the mutant stays between 48% and 53%.
options: Correct: the label moves out of short pieces in the normal strain only.
The mutant hardly changes (53% to 48%) while the normal strain drops to 3%.
The mutant falls by 5 percentage points, the normal strain by 48.
The normal strain's share falls, from 51% to 3%.

why.correct: Because the strands are antiparallel and DNA polymerase adds only to a 3′ end, one new strand (leading) grows continuously toward the fork while the other (lagging) is made in short Okazaki fragments. So roughly half of the new DNA starts out in short pieces.
options: Correct: leading strand long, lagging strand in fragments.
Cells that were not copying DNA would take up no label at all, so they would not add unlabeled long DNA to the count.
If separation broke strands, the mutant would lose label from long DNA as well, and its numbers would not stay steady.
If both strands were made in pieces, nearly all label would start in short pieces; in the mutant it stays near half, so the other half was never short.

why.correct: The mutant still makes short pieces and long DNA, but the short pieces are never joined. Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments, so a failed ligase leaves them separate.
options: Correct: fragments are made but not joined.
Without helicase the strands would not open, and almost no new DNA would be labeled at all.
Without primase no new fragments could start, so the mutant would have fewer short pieces, not a steady half.
Without topoisomerase twisting would stall the forks; the problem here is joining, not unwinding.

why.correct: If the mutant behaves normally whenever its enzyme works, the strains differ in nothing else that matters here; the effect at 42 °C must come from that enzyme failing.
options: Correct: it is a control for other differences between the two strains.
The normal strain joins its fragments at 42 °C, so the temperature itself does not damage DNA copying.
The normal strain was tested at 42 °C; this test is about the mutant.
Both strains make short pieces whenever they copy DNA; the mutant's defect is in joining them.

why.correct: Percent change = (18 − 51) ÷ 51 × 100 = −64.7%, a decrease of about 65%. (The drop is 33 percentage points; as a percent of the starting value it is 65%.)

Expected errors = base pairs copied × error rate = 4.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> × 1 × 10<sup>−7</sup> = 0.46 errors per genome copy, about one new mistake every two divisions (the normal strain: 0.00046, about one in 2,000 divisions).

Losing proofreading raises errors 100-fold, losing mismatch repair 1,000-fold, and losing both 100,000-fold (100 × 1,000). Each system catches most of what is left by the step before, so their effects multiply.
options: Correct: the double mutant is worse than either single mutant by about the other system's factor.
Losing mismatch repair (10<sup>−7</sup>) raises errors more than losing proofreading (10<sup>−8</sup>).
Losing both (10<sup>−5</sup>) is far worse than losing one, so they are not redundant.
Mutant P, with mismatch repair working, still has 100 times more errors than normal, so mismatch repair does not fix everything.

why.correct: Mutant M shows that losing mismatch repair raises the error rate about 1,000-fold. In a tissue whose cells divide often, like the colon lining, more errors reach genes such as tumor suppressors and the genes that drive the cell cycle (topic 4.6).
options: Correct: a higher mutation rate makes the changes that cause cancer more likely.
Mismatch repair fixes base errors; it is not a checkpoint protein that holds the cycle.
The table shows accuracy, not speed; nothing suggests copying gets faster.
Mismatch repair corrects mispaired bases in new DNA; it has nothing to do with removing viruses.

why.correct: DNA polymerase checks each base it adds and removes a wrong one before moving on. Mismatch repair enzymes later find mispaired bases, cut out a stretch of the new strand and fill it in again.
options: Correct: same goal, different time and different enzymes.
Both systems fix copying mistakes (mispaired bases), and ligase does not add bases.
Both systems act on the new strand, which is the one with the copying mistake.
This reverses the timing: proofreading happens as each base is added, at the fork.

why.correct: DNA polymerase needs a free 3′ –OH to attach the next nucleotide to. Primase, which can start a chain, lays down a short RNA primer that provides it.
options: Correct: the primer supplies the starting 3′ end.
Helicase unwinds the helix; the primer is a short stretch of RNA paired to the template.
The primer is removed and replaced by DNA, so it does not mark strands for repair.
DNA polymerase always builds 5′ to 3′; a primer does not change its direction.

why.correct: Pair each base (T–A, A–T, C–G, G–C) and make the new strand antiparallel: the template's 3′ end lines up with the new strand's 5′ end, so the new strand reads 5′-ATGGCCTA-3′, built from 5′ to 3′.
options: Correct: complementary bases, antiparallel, written 5′ to 3′.
The bases are right, but the ends are labeled as if the strands ran parallel; they run in opposite directions.
This is the template itself, rewritten from 5′ to 3′; the new strand is its complement.
U belongs in RNA; DNA polymerase builds DNA, which uses T.

why.correct: Unwinding at the fork overwinds the DNA ahead of it. Topoisomerase cuts and rejoins the DNA to relieve that strain; without it, tension builds until helicase can no longer open the helix.
options: Correct: topoisomerase relieves the twisting that unwinding causes.
Single-strand binding proteins and the new strands keep the templates apart; topoisomerase works ahead of the fork.
Replacing primers is the job of DNA polymerase I.
Sealing fragments is the job of DNA ligase.

why.correct: The template must be single-stranded before a primer can pair with it; DNA polymerase III needs the primer's 3′ end; the fragment grows until it reaches the previous fragment, whose RNA primer DNA polymerase I then replaces; ligase seals the last nick.

Linear chromosomes lose a little DNA from their ends each time they are copied. Telomeres are buffers of repeated DNA with no genes, so early losses are harmless; once they run short, cells stop dividing. Telomerase, active in germ cells, some dividing body cells and many cancer cells, rebuilds them.

variables.name: Length of the telomeres at the ends of each chromosome
variables.why: At each end, the last RNA primer leaves a gap that cannot be filled with DNA, so the ends shorten a little at every copy unless telomerase extends them.

variables.name: Number of genes on each chromosome, during the early divisions
variables.why: Telomeres are repeats with no genes, so early shortening removes only repeats, which is the point of having them.

variables.name: Chance that a cell stops dividing
variables.why: When telomeres become very short, the cell treats the ends as damaged DNA and permanently stops dividing.

why.correct: Two forks copy 2 × 50 = 100 base pairs per second. 150,000,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500,000 s ÷ 3,600 = 417 h, about 17 days. Real S phase takes a few hours because each chromosome has thousands of origins working at once.

DNA polymerase I fills a primer's gap by extending the DNA behind it. At the very end of a lagging strand there is nothing behind the last primer, so that stretch stays single-stranded and is lost. A circle has no ends, so every primer gap has DNA behind it.
options: Correct: the end-replication problem comes from primers plus 5′-to-3′ synthesis.
The ends are opened and mostly copied; only the last primer's stretch on the lagging strand is lost.
Ligase joins DNA; it does not cut chromosome ends.
Forks reach the ends; the problem is filling the last primer's gap, not timing.

why.correct: Every Okazaki fragment needs its own primer (primase), its primer later replaced with DNA (DNA polymerase I), and a nick sealed (ligase). The leading strand needs this only once, at its start.
options: Correct: one primer per fragment.
Correct: one nick to seal per fragment.
Helicase opens the fork once for both strands; it works continuously, not once per fragment.
Topoisomerase acts on the DNA ahead of the fork, which serves both strands equally.
Correct: one primer to replace per fragment.

why.correct: The RNA is built by pairing with the template, so it is complementary and antiparallel to it: RNA 5′-AUG… pairs with B 3′-TAC…. That makes B the template and A the coding strand.
options: Correct: complementary and antiparallel to the RNA means template.
Matching the RNA's sequence is the mark of the coding strand, not the template.
Running in the same direction as the RNA is another sign of the coding strand.
Which strand is drawn below is a drawing choice; the template is identified by pairing.

why.correct: RNA grows 5′ to 3′, so the polymerase reads its template 3′ to 5′. Strand B's 3′ end is on the left, beside the promoter, so the enzyme moves left to right, away from the promoter.
options: Correct: template read 3′ to 5′, RNA built 5′ to 3′.
Reading the template 5′ to 3′ would build RNA 3′ to 5′, which RNA polymerase cannot do.
B's 3′ end is on the left in the model, so moving 3′ to 5′ means moving right.
One enzyme builds the RNA from its 5′ end onward, starting at the promoter.

why.correct: Pair each base of strand A (A→U, T→A, G→C, C→G) and make the RNA antiparallel. Strand A's 3′ end is on the right, so the RNA's 5′ end is opposite it: reading strand B's bases from right to left gives 5′-UGCUAACGGCAU-3′.
options: Correct: complementary to A, antiparallel, written 5′ to 3′.
This is the RNA made from strand B, the real template.
This is the complement of A written left to right, which lists it 3′ to 5′ with the ends mislabeled.
RNA uses U, not T; this is strand B written backward.

why.correct: RNA polymerase starts at the start site next to the promoter and adds each nucleotide to the 3′ end of the chain, so the 5′ end is made first.
options: Correct: the 5′ end is the start of the chain.
The 3′ end is the last part added; the chain grows at its 3′ end.
The second nucleotide was added just after the first, at the 5′ end.
The enzyme binds the promoter, to the left of this stretch, not the middle of the RNA.

why.correct: Only the exons remain after splicing: 210 + 135 + 96 + 489 = 930 nucleotides.
930 − 834 = 96, exactly the length of exon 3. Joining exons 1, 2 and 4 is alternative splicing: the same pre-mRNA, spliced in two ways in two tissues.
options: Correct: the difference matches exon 3, and the DNA is unchanged.
Keeping intron 3 (870) and dropping exons 3 and 4 (585) would give 345 + 870 = 1,215, not 834.
Stopping inside intron 3 would leave out exon 4 (489 nucleotides), not 96.
The stem says the DNA is the same in both cell types; the difference arises after copying.

why.correct: 7,070 nucleotides is the full pre-mRNA. Bacterial genes rarely have introns of this kind, and bacteria lack spliceosomes, so the introns are never removed and the RNA no longer carries the protein's instructions in one continuous stretch.
options: Correct: transcription works, but there is no splicing.
An RNA exactly as long as gene K's pre-mRNA shows the bacteria did copy the human gene.
Bacteria do not splice at all; they neither remove introns nor exons.
Bacteria have no nucleus, and the RNA's length matches the unspliced gene, not an extra tail.

why.correct: RNA uses U where DNA uses T. Labeled uridine goes into RNA, so the counts follow RNA made during the pulse; thymidine would label new DNA instead.
options: Correct: the label is specific to RNA.
Speed of uptake is not the reason; the base decides which molecule is labeled.
Thymidine goes into DNA, not protein; the issue is that it would not label RNA.
The excess unlabeled uridine ends the pulse; the label stays in the RNA already made.

why.correct: At 10 minutes almost all label (48 of 49) is in the nucleus. Over two hours the nuclear label falls while the cytoplasmic label rises to 18, so labeled RNA made in the nucleus is moving out.
options: Correct: label appears in the nucleus first, then in the cytoplasm.
The cytoplasm starts with almost no label (1), so RNA is not made there first.
If both made RNA, the cytoplasm would be labeled from the start; it was not.
The cytoplasm's label rises from 1 to 18, so RNA does move.

why.correct: Much of each pre-mRNA is intron, which spliceosomes remove in the nucleus; the cut-out introns are broken down, so their label is lost instead of reaching the cytoplasm.
options: Correct: label in introns never leaves the nucleus.
Cells do not turn their RNA back into DNA as part of making mRNA.
The cap and tail stay on the mRNA when it is exported.
Copying labeled RNA would not remove its label; RNA is made from DNA templates.

why.correct: Eukaryotes have three RNA polymerases. At this dose α-amanitin blocks only RNA polymerase II, which makes pre-mRNA; RNA polymerases I and III, which make ribosomal RNA and tRNA, keep working.
options: Correct: the label that remains is in RNAs that RNA polymerase II does not make.
The stem says the dose blocks RNA polymerase II; a different source is the better explanation.
Uridine goes into RNA, not DNA.
Ribosomes build proteins; they do not make mRNA.

why.correct: Total at 120 min = 24 + 18 = 42 thousand counts. Cytoplasm share = 18 ÷ 42 × 100 = 42.9%, about 43%.
Transcription copies a gene's information from DNA into RNA. Copying the whole chromosome is replication; building the protein is the next step (topic 6.4); cutting out introns is RNA processing.
options: Correct: DNA → RNA.
Copying the whole chromosome is DNA replication.
Building the protein is the step after transcription, taught in 6.4.
Removing introns is splicing, part of RNA processing after transcription.

why.correct: RNA polymerase starts chains on its own at a promoter, unwinds a short stretch of DNA itself, and copies only the template strand of the genes it reads, adding U opposite A.
options: Correct: no primer is needed to start RNA.
Correct: only a gene's template strand is copied, and only when the gene is used.
Both polymerases build 5′ to 3′.
RNA polymerase opens the DNA itself and needs no primer.
RNA uses uracil, so U is placed opposite A.

why.correct: The promoter, including the TATA box, is where proteins gather and place RNA polymerase II at the start site. Without that binding, the gene is rarely transcribed.
options: Correct: the promoter controls where and whether copying starts.
The promoter lies before the start site and is not part of the mRNA; damaging it reduces starting, not the first exon.
Splicing depends on sequences at the exon-intron boundaries, not the promoter.
Without a recognizable promoter, RNA polymerase is not positioned at the gene at all.

why.correct: The poly-A tail is added after copying and helps export and protect the mRNA. Blocking it reduces the mRNA that reaches the cytoplasm, without changing how often genes are copied or what the gene contains.

variables.name: Amount of mature mRNA reaching the cytoplasm
variables.why: The tail helps mRNA leave the nucleus and protects it from being broken down, so less mRNA reaches the cytoplasm intact.

variables.name: Rate at which RNA polymerase II starts copying genes
variables.why: Starting depends on the promoter and the proteins that bind it, which come before the tail is added.

variables.name: Length of the introns in each pre-mRNA
variables.why: Introns are encoded in the DNA; the drug changes what is added to the RNA's 3′ end, not the gene.

why.correct: Binding the promoter positions the enzyme; it must open the DNA before it can read the template; it builds the RNA until it copies the terminator, which signals release.
Some genes make RNAs that work as RNA. tRNA folds into a compact shape and brings amino acids to the ribosome; ribosomal RNA forms much of the ribosome itself.
options: Correct: tRNA is a working RNA, not a set of instructions.
mRNA is by definition the RNA that carries a protein's instructions.
Pre-mRNA is processed into mRNA, which is then used to build a protein.
Joined exons are mature mRNA, used to build a protein.

why.correct: RNA polymerase reads its template 3′ to 5′. Moving left to right on one strand means its 3′ end is on the left; moving right to left means the 3′ end is on the right, which is the other strand. So the genes have templates on opposite strands.
options: Correct: opposite directions require opposite template strands.
One strand has a single 3′ to 5′ direction, so the two genes could not both be read along it in opposite directions.
Every template is read 3′ to 5′ and every RNA is built 5′ to 3′.
Each gene has its own promoter at its start; for gene 1 that is the left end.

why.correct: Start at the first AUG (Met) and read in threes: CCU Pro, UGG Trp, AAG Lys, UGC Cys, then UAG, a stop codon, ends the chain.
options: Correct: AUG to the codon before UAG.
ACG lies before the start codon, so it is not read.
UAG is a stop codon; CAU after it is not read.
The start codon AUG is read too, and puts methionine first.

why.correct: Nucleotides 10-12 are the third codon read from AUG, UGG (Trp). With A at position 12 it reads UGA, a stop codon, so the chain ends after Met-Pro.
options: Correct: UGG → UGA turns tryptophan's codon into a stop.
Some single changes leave the amino acid the same, but UGA is a stop codon, so this one shortens the chain.
Ribosomes do not skip codons; a stop codon ends the chain there.
UGA is not a codon for glutamic acid (GAA or GAG); it is a stop codon.

why.correct: The anticodon pairs with the codon antiparallel: codon 5′-UGG-3′ pairs with anticodon 3′-ACC-5′ (U with A, G with C, G with C).
options: Correct: complementary and antiparallel.
This repeats the codon; an anticodon is complementary to it.
The bases are complementary, but written this way the anticodon would run parallel to the codon.
tRNA is RNA, so it carries U, not T; and T does not pair with U.

why.correct: The mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template: 5′-CCU-3′ pairs with 3′-GGA-5′ in the DNA.
options: Correct: template is complementary to the mRNA, read 3′ to 5′.
The bases are right, but written 5′ to 3′ they would pair in the wrong order with the codon.
3′-CCT-5′ matches the mRNA's letters, which is what the coding strand does (and in the other direction).
DNA has T, not U.

why.correct: The chain has five amino acids (Met-Pro-Trp-Lys-Cys). Each peptide bond joins two neighbors, so there are 5 − 1 = 4 peptide bonds.
Poly-U contains only UUU codons, whatever frame is read, and it raised phenylalanine incorporation from 40 to 13,900 counts while the others stayed near background.
options: Correct: only phenylalanine rose with poly-U.
Leucine stayed at 70 counts with poly-U, close to background.
A stop codon would give no long chains; poly-U gave heavy phenylalanine incorporation.
Only phenylalanine rose; the code is specific.

why.correct: UCUCUC… read in non-overlapping triplets is UCU-CUC-UCU-CUC…, two different codons in turn, matching the alternating serine and leucine. A two-letter code would read UC-UC-UC…, one codon repeated, giving one amino acid.
options: Correct: an odd-length codon makes the two codons alternate.
Read in twos, every codon would be UC, giving one amino acid repeated, not two alternating.
Triplets from UCUC… alternate between UCU and CUC; they are not one repeated codon.
Four bases read singly could code for only four amino acids, and the poly-U, poly-A and poly-C results each give one amino acid, not a mixture.

why.correct: With no added RNA, incorporation is 30-50 counts for every amino acid. A rise far above this, such as 13,900, can then be credited to the added RNA.
options: Correct: a negative control and baseline.
The extract does contain ribosomes and tRNAs; they are needed in every tube.
Low counts in these tubes do not show the label works; the high counts in the other tubes do.
Nothing passes from one tube to another; each tube is separate.

why.correct: Read in triplets, ACACAC… gives ACA-CAC-ACA-CAC…, so threonine and histidine alternate in one chain, just as UCUC… gave alternating serine and leucine.
options: Correct: the same logic as the UCUC… result.
One RNA read in one frame gives one chain with both codons in turn.
The next codon after ACA is CAC, so histidine follows threonine.
Poly-U and the other artificial RNAs also lacked AUG but were translated in this system, so a start codon is not needed here.

why.correct: A secreted protein starts with a signal peptide that directs the ribosome to the ER. Once the chain is threaded into the ER, an enzyme there cuts the signal peptide off, so the finished protein is shorter.
options: Correct: the first ~20 amino acids are removed inside the ER.
Every tube had all twenty amino acids; the difference depends on the ER being present.
The protease could not reach protein inside the sealed vesicles; that is why tube 2's protein was protected.
Speed does not change the length; a ribosome reads the mRNA to its stop codon.

why.correct: In tube 2 the protein entered the vesicles; in tube 3 the same protein, finished first, did not. So entry happens during translation: the signal peptide emerges first and brings the ribosome to the ER, and the chain is threaded in as it grows.
options: Correct: targeting happens as the chain is made.
Nothing in the data points to a need for an intact cell; the timing of adding the vesicles is the only difference from tube 2.
The same kind of vesicles took in the protein in tube 2; nothing suggests tube 3's were damaged.
The protein is the same size as in tube 1, and the same protein entered in tube 2, so size is not the reason.

why.correct: Removing the 60 nucleotides (20 codons) after the start codon removes the signal peptide. The protein is still made (22 kDa) but is not taken into the vesicles, so the signal at the start of the chain is what directs it to the ER.
options: Correct: without its beginning, the protein stays outside.
Only the start of the coding sequence was removed, and that is what stopped entry.
The protein is 22 kDa because its first 20 amino acids were never coded, not because they were cut off.
The start codon was kept (the deletion is after it), and a 22 kDa protein was made.

why.correct: 24 − 22 = 2 kDa = 2,000 Da. 2,000 ÷ 110 = 18.2, about 18 amino acids, a typical signal peptide length (and close to the 20 codons deleted in tube 4).
Each synthetase recognizes one amino acid and the tRNAs for it, and links them using ATP. This charging step is what actually connects the code to the amino acids.
options: Correct: the synthetase charges tRNAs.
Peptide bonds are formed by the ribosome (its rRNA).
Codon-anticodon pairing is base pairing inside the ribosome, not an enzyme's job.
A release factor frees the chain at a stop codon.

why.correct: The bacterial ribosomes, tRNAs and synthetases turned the human codons into the human amino acid sequence, so the two read the code the same way. A shared, nearly universal code is best explained by descent from a common ancestor.
options: Correct: same code, shared ancestry.
Bacteria do not normally make insulin; the point is that they read the human gene correctly.
The stem says the gene was given without introns; bacteria lack spliceosomes.
Insulin is an animal hormone; the bacteria made it only because they were given the gene.

why.correct: A tRNA must bind the A site before its amino acid can be joined; the bond transfers the chain to it; moving the ribosome shifts that tRNA into the P site and the empty one into the E site, from which it leaves.

A retrovirus reverses part of the central dogma: reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, which joins the host's DNA and is then used like any gene. Blocking that enzyme blocks everything downstream of it.

variables.name: Amount of viral DNA made from the viral RNA
variables.why: Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme that copies the viral RNA genome into DNA; blocking it stops that copy.

variables.name: Amount of new viral protein made by the cell
variables.why: Viral genes are transcribed and translated from the DNA copy built into the host's DNA, so without it few viral proteins are made.

variables.name: Base sequence of the RNA genome inside the virus particles that entered
variables.why: The drug blocks copying; it does not change the RNA already inside the particles.

why.correct: Bacteria have no nucleus, so ribosomes reach the mRNA as soon as its 5′ end appears (coupled transcription and translation), and several ribosomes can follow one another along it (a polyribosome).
options: Correct: transcription and translation are coupled.
Correct: polyribosomes form in bacteria and eukaryotes alike.
Bacterial genes rarely have spliceosome-removed introns.
Bacteria have no nucleus and so no nuclear pores.
Long poly-A tails added to every mRNA are a eukaryotic processing step.

why.correct: Stop codons are not matched by any tRNA in a normal cell. A protein release factor binds the A site instead, the bond holding the chain to the last tRNA is broken, and the subunits separate from the mRNA.
options: Correct: termination by a release factor.
Stop codons have no matching tRNA, so no amino acid is added.
UAG ends the chain; it is not skipped.
The subunits separate; a new ribosome may start again at the start codon, but the finished one does not back up.

why.correct: From the first AUG the codons are AUG-CAU-GCC-AAA-UGG…; from the second they are AUG-CCA-AAU-GG…. Four is not a multiple of three, so every codon is grouped differently: a new reading frame.
options: Correct: the grouping into triplets shifts.
AUG always codes for methionine; the change comes from how later bases are grouped.
The ribosome reads every nucleotide in order, three at a time; it does not skip any.
Each codon is read on its own; one amino acid does not determine the next.

why.correct: 300 amino acids need 300 codons (the start codon codes for the first one, methionine), and the stop codon adds one more codon with no amino acid: 301 × 3 = 903 nucleotides.
With glycerol, adding lactose takes activity from 3 to 1,020 units. With glucose, it goes only from 2 to 55.
options: Correct: strong induction without glucose, weak with it.
The increase is about 1,000 units without glucose but about 50 with it.
This reverses the two media.
Activity rises from 3 to 1,020 when lactose is added to glycerol medium, a large effect.

why.correct: 1,020 ÷ 3 = 340. The operon is induced about 340-fold when lactose is present and glucose is absent.

cAMP is 18% with glucose, and adding cAMP restores activity to 780 units in the presence of glucose. cAMP-CAP is an activator that helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter; without it, removing the repressor gives only weak transcription.
options: Correct: low cAMP explains the glucose effect, and adding cAMP reverses it.
If glucose held the repressor on, adding cAMP would not restore activity to 780.
The glycolysis enzyme is unaffected, and adding cAMP restores activity, so the enzyme is not being destroyed.
Gene copies do not change with the food; adding cAMP restores activity with the same cells.

why.correct: Its activity stays between 495 and 530 units in all five media. Genes whose products every cell needs all the time, like this glycolysis enzyme, are constitutive (housekeeping) genes.
options: Correct: no change with any sugar or with cAMP.
Its activity does not rise with lactose (510 vs 495).
Its activity does not fall with glucose (530).
Genes in one operon rise and fall together; this enzyme does not follow β-galactosidase.

why.correct: Lactose still removes the repressor, but without cAMP the activator CAP cannot bind and boost transcription, so the operon behaves as it does when glucose keeps cAMP low: weakly on.
options: Correct: induction needs both the repressor off and cAMP-CAP on.
Removing the repressor is not enough for full activity; the data with glucose show that low cAMP limits it.
cAMP acts through CAP, not the repressor; lactose still releases the repressor.
Nothing in the data links cAMP to growth rate, and the gene would be activated less, not more.

why.correct: mRNA is lowest (1) with 85% methylation and acetylation 1.0, and highest (40) with 18% methylation and acetylation 5.0.
options: Correct: unmarked DNA and acetylated histones go with an active gene.
The highest mRNA comes with the lowest methylation.
Drug H barely changes methylation (83%); drug M lowers it. Drug M also raises acetylation a little.
Drug H raises mRNA six-fold.

why.correct: Histones bind DNA through positive charges. Acetyl groups neutralize some of those charges, so the histones grip DNA less tightly, chromatin opens, and transcription factors and RNA polymerase can reach the promoter.
options: Correct: acetylation opens chromatin.
Acetylation here is on histone proteins, and the stem says the DNA sequence did not change.
Drug H left methylation almost unchanged (83%), so it did not remove the methyl marks.
Opening chromatin makes genes accessible; it does not deliver the polymerase or act on every gene equally.

why.correct: 40 ÷ 14 = 2.86, about 2.9. Adding drug H to drug M nearly triples the mRNA, more than either drug alone, so the two marks act together.

The pattern of marks, and with it the gene's activity, was passed to daughter cells, while the stem says the sequence is unchanged. That is epigenetic inheritance: cells copy methylation patterns onto new DNA by marking the new strand to match the old one.
options: Correct: inherited marks, same sequence.
The DNA sequence was checked and unchanged.
The drug was removed and diluted out over 20 divisions; once the marks are gone, cells copy the unmethylated pattern.
Gene T was silent before treatment, so it is not on in every cell regardless of marks.

why.correct: Methyl groups on C's in a promoter are recognized by proteins that bring in histone-modifying enzymes and compact the chromatin, and they can also prevent some transcription factors from binding.
options: Correct: methylation leads to closed chromatin and blocked binding.
Methylation adds a small group to a base; it does not break the DNA.
Methylated C still pairs with G; methylation does not change base pairing.
RNA polymerase does not consume methyl groups.

why.correct: Removing region E drops activity from 100% to 4%: region E greatly increases transcription, as an enhancer does.
options: Correct: without region E, activity is 4%.
Construct 5 has region E but no promoter and is almost silent, so region E is not the promoter.
A silencer would raise activity when removed; activity fell instead.
Activity drops 25-fold without region E.

why.correct: Activator transcription factors bind the enhancer; the DNA loops so they contact the proteins at the promoter and help RNA polymerase start. Looping works from either side and in either orientation.
options: Correct: looping brings distant enhancers to the promoter.
Construct 4 places region E after the gene, where copying from it could not pass through the reporter's start.
If region E made a protein, turning it end to end would wreck its coding sequence; it is a binding site, not a gene.
In construct 1, region E lies 2,000 bp before the promoter and is not transcribed into the reporter mRNA.

why.correct: The same DNA was put into both cell types. An enhancer works only where the activator that binds it is present, so the difference lies in which transcription factors each cell type makes.
options: Correct: same DNA, different proteins available to read it.
The construct carries its own region E, so the kidney cells had it.
Kidney cells give 2-3% with every construct with a promoter, so they can make some reporter; what they lack is the boost from region E.
Nothing in the data points to methylation; the simplest difference is the activator.

why.correct: With region E but no promoter, activity is 0.5%. An enhancer increases transcription from a promoter but cannot replace it.
options: Correct: it is a control for the promoter.
Construct 5 keeps the spacer; it removes the promoter.
Construct 3 tests orientation.
Every construct was tested in both cell types; construct 5 is about the promoter.

why.correct: In an operon, structural genes for one job sit together after a shared promoter and operator, so they are switched on and off together and copied as one mRNA.
options: Correct: promoter + operator + structural genes.
That is a repressor.
That describes alternative splicing (topic 6.3).
That is an enhancer.

why.correct: The trp operon is repressible: its end product, tryptophan, activates the repressor. When tryptophan is plentiful, the cell stops making the enzymes that build it. Other operons, such as lac, do not respond to tryptophan.

variables.name: Amount of trp repressor bound to the trp operator
variables.why: Tryptophan acts as a corepressor: it binds the repressor, activating it so it binds the operator.

variables.name: Amount of trp operon mRNA made
variables.why: The active repressor on the operator blocks RNA polymerase, so the operon is switched off.

variables.name: Amount of lac operon mRNA made (no lactose in either medium)
variables.why: Tryptophan does not act on the lac repressor or on CAP; with no lactose, the lac operon stays off before and after the move.

why.correct: Lactose normally works only by pulling the repressor off the operator. If the repressor cannot bind, the operon is on whether or not lactose is present (and cAMP is high on glycerol).
options: Correct: a repressor that cannot bind leaves the operon always on.
The repressor blocks RNA polymerase; it does not help it bind.
The inducer's only job is to remove the repressor, which is already off the DNA.
The repressor gene is outside the operon, but its protein controls the operon, so a broken repressor matters.

why.correct: Induction depends on allolactose binding the repressor and changing its shape. A repressor that ignores the inducer stays on the operator, so the operon stays off even with lactose.
options: Correct: the operon cannot be induced.
Ignoring the inducer means it stays bound, so the operon stays off, not on.
CAP increases transcription only when the operator is free; it cannot push past a bound repressor.
The stem says the repressor binds the operator normally.

why.correct: Repressible operons usually code for enzymes that build something (here tryptophan). They are on until the product accumulates; the product (corepressor) activates the repressor, which then binds the operator.
options: Correct: on by default, off with plenty of product.
Correct: the corepressor turns the repressor on.
An inducer inactivating a repressor describes an inducible operon such as lac.
Breaking down a food is typical of inducible operons; repressible ones usually build a product.
A bound repressor blocks transcription.

why.correct: The protein is unchanged, and the difference lies far from the gene, in a regulatory region (an enhancer). It changes when and how much the gene is transcribed, and the amount of gene product decides whether the person can digest lactose.
options: Correct: regulation, not the protein, differs.
The stem says the protein is identical, so the coding sequence is not the difference.
Lactase persistence is inherited through a DNA difference; it is not caused by childhood milk drinking.
The difference is a change in a regulatory sequence, not an extra copy of the gene.

why.correct: Negative regulation means a bound protein reduces transcription (the repressor on the operator). Positive regulation means a bound protein increases it (cAMP-CAP near the promoter).
options: Correct: the repressor turns off; CAP turns up.
This swaps them: binding of the repressor lowers transcription.
CAP binding raises transcription, which makes it positive regulation.
Repressor binding lowers transcription, which makes it negative regulation.

why.correct: Albumin is high only in liver, insulin only in islets and myosin only in muscle (others below 1%), while the glycolysis enzyme is 48-100% in every tissue.
options: Correct: three tissue-specific genes and one used everywhere.
The glycolysis enzyme is 48% or more in every tissue, so it is not limited to one.
Albumin is 100% in liver and under 1% elsewhere, far outside the error bars.
This reverses the pattern: the glycolysis enzyme is the one found everywhere.

why.correct: Almost every cell in the body carries the same genome. The near-zero bar shows the gene is not being transcribed in liver, not that it is missing; testing the liver cells' DNA would find the gene.
options: Correct: absence of mRNA is not absence of the gene.
Many genes are present but silent; differential gene expression is the rule.
0.1% is at the level of background, and mRNA alone would not show the hormone is made and released.
Cells do not discard unused genes; nuclei from specialized cells can still direct a whole new animal.

why.correct: Glycolysis is a housekeeping job that nearly all cells need, so its enzymes' genes are expressed in nearly every cell type, though at different levels.
options: Correct: a housekeeping gene, used everywhere.
Every cell carries this gene, like every other gene.
mRNAs are made and used inside the cell that transcribes them.
Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, and genes are not all copied in any one cell.

why.correct: MyoD is a master regulator: it binds enhancers of many muscle genes and switches them on together, and it activates more muscle transcription factors. Skin cells carry those genes, so MyoD can turn many of them into muscle-like cells, as was first shown in 1987.
options: Correct: one factor can launch a whole coordinated program.
A cell's genes are not fixed off forever; a new transcription factor can switch on genes it targets.
Switching programs does not delete genes; DNA is not lost.
MyoD binds the enhancers of muscle genes; liver and islet genes need their own activators.

why.correct: 100 ÷ 0.5 = 200. Liver cells transcribe the albumin gene about 200 times as much as islet cells do.
With extra miR-X, mRNA falls to 0.45 and protein to 0.20, while transcription stays at 0.98, essentially unchanged.
options: Correct: a larger drop in protein than mRNA, transcription unchanged.
Transcription is 0.98, the same as untreated cells within error.
Protein P falls to 0.20.
Protein P falls; it is blocking miR-X that raises it.

why.correct: A microRNA is loaded into a protein complex and guided by base pairing to its target mRNA, where it reduces translation and speeds the mRNA's breakdown. That fits lower mRNA, even lower protein and unchanged transcription.
options: Correct: post-transcriptional regulation by base pairing.
Transcription is unchanged, so miR-X does not act at the promoter.
MicroRNAs are not translated; they act as RNA.
Methylation would silence transcription, which did not change.

why.correct: Extra miR-X has almost no effect (0.97, 0.95) on an mRNA it cannot pair with. So the effect requires complementary pairing at that site; it is not a side effect of adding RNA to cells.
options: Correct: a control for specificity.
The stem says the protein is unchanged; the three bases lie outside the coding part.
That is shown by the row where the cells' own miR-X is blocked.
Transcription of the protein P gene is unchanged in every row.

why.correct: Removing the cells' own miR-X nearly doubles protein P, so at normal levels miR-X is already holding protein P down.
options: Correct: taking away the natural regulator raises its target.
Adding extra miR-X shows what more of it can do, not what the normal amount does.
That row tests pairing with added miR-X; it does not remove the cells' own.
Untreated cells are the baseline; they cannot show an effect by themselves.

why.correct: The normal curve is 20.2 at 40% and 13.5 at 50%. 15 lies about three quarters of the way down that step: 40 + 10 × (20.2 − 15) ÷ (20.2 − 13.5) ≈ 48; reading the curve gives about 47%.

With twice as much Bicoid, the level stays above 15 units farther back: the four-copy curve is 18.1 at 60% and 12.2 at 70%, so the edge moves to about 65%. Real embryos from such mothers have enlarged head regions shifted backward.
options: Correct: more morphogen moves each threshold away from the source.
More Bicoid raises the level at every position, so the region grows rather than shrinks.
Cells respond to the Bicoid level they experience, not just to which genes they carry.
The four-copy curve falls below 15 units by about 65%, so the back part still lacks hunchback.

why.correct: Bicoid is a morphogen: target genes have enhancers that need different amounts of it, so high, middle and low levels switch on different combinations of genes, giving different regions their identities.
options: Correct: concentration thresholds become positional information.
Every cell has the same genome; what differs is which genes are switched on.
No DNA is destroyed; genes are left off, not removed.
The model is about which genes are transcribed at each Bicoid level, not about division rate.

why.correct: Bicoid mRNA is placed in the egg by the mother's cells before fertilization. With none, there is no gradient, hunchback is not switched on at the front, and head and thorax do not form. The father's genes arrive too late to make the gradient.
options: Correct: a maternal-effect gene; the mother's genotype decides.
The gradient comes from mRNA the mother puts into the egg, before the embryo's own genes are used.
With no Bicoid there is no high level anywhere, so no head forms at either end.
Every embryo depends on the mother's mRNA, so the father's copies do not rescue any of them.

why.correct: A fertilized egg and the cells of the first few divisions are totipotent. Cells of the inner cell mass of an early embryo are pluripotent: they can become any cell of the body, but not the placenta.
options: Correct: totipotent is the broadest potential.
This reverses the two terms.
Totipotent cells exist only at the very start of development; adult stem cells are more limited.
Both divide by mitosis; meiosis is for making gametes.

why.correct: A whole tadpole needs every kind of gene. Since a specialized cell's nucleus could direct one, specialization keeps the genome intact and works by switching genes on and off; the egg's cytoplasm reset which genes were used.
options: Correct: differentiated cells keep their whole genome.
If intestine cells kept only intestine genes, they could not supply the genes for muscle, nerve and skin.
The egg's nucleus was destroyed; the tadpole's genes came from the transplanted nucleus.
The egg cytoplasm has no nucleus to supply genes; the result shows nothing was lost.

why.correct: Protein breakdown is post-translational regulation: tagging proteins for the proteasome removes them on cue. Blocking it leaves proteins such as cyclins in place, which holds cells in mitosis; transcription is not the step affected.

variables.name: Amount of mitotic cyclin in cells an hour after they reach metaphase
variables.why: Cyclins are tagged and broken down by the proteasome to end mitosis; with the proteasome blocked, they stay.

variables.name: Number of cells that complete mitosis and divide
variables.why: Cells need cyclin breakdown to exit mitosis, so they stall instead of finishing division.

variables.name: Transcription rate of the cyclin gene
variables.why: The drug acts after translation, on protein breakdown, not on transcription of the gene.

why.correct: Cutting a finished polypeptide to activate it is a post-translational modification, like adding phosphate groups or sugars; it controls when and where the active protein appears.
options: Correct: the change happens to the protein, after translation.
Splicing happens to pre-mRNA in the nucleus, not to proteins in the Golgi.
Histone marks affect transcription, not the processing of a protein.
Enhancers act on transcription; this cut happens to the finished chain.

why.correct: Hox genes are master regulatory genes: their products are transcription factors that tell a body segment what to become by switching on whole sets of genes. Switched on in the head, the thorax Hox gene sets off the leg program there.
options: Correct: one regulatory gene controls many others, so a whole structure changes.
A single structural protein cannot build a leg; Hox proteins regulate many genes.
All cells have the same genes; the difference is which are switched on.
Division speed does not explain a structure as organized as a leg.

why.correct: A lens forms wherever the optic cup is, so the cup causes it; it still forms through a filter that blocks cells, so the signal is a molecule that diffuses. This is induction: one tissue's signals change gene expression in a neighbor.
options: Correct: induction by a diffusing signal.
The filter blocks cells, yet a lens forms, so no cells were carried over.
Side skin forms a lens only when the optic cup is placed under it.
The filter prevents contact, yet a lens forms, so contact is not required.

why.correct: MicroRNAs and splicing act on RNA that has already been made, so they are post-transcriptional. Histone acetylation, activators at enhancers and DNA methylation all affect whether transcription happens.
options: Correct: it acts on an existing mRNA.
Correct: it acts on an existing pre-mRNA.
Histone acetylation changes access to DNA, before transcription.
Activators control whether transcription starts.
Promoter methylation silences transcription.

why.correct: Induction starts with a signal, whose pathway changes which transcription factors are active; those factors switch on a coordinated set of genes, and their products give the cell its specialized structure and function.
In strain B the fourth codon changes from GAA to GAG. Both code for glutamic acid, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged: a silent mutation.
options: Strain A's deleted base shifts the reading frame, so the chain changes after alanine and stops early.
Correct: GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid.
Strain C's third codon becomes UGA, a stop codon, so the chain ends after two amino acids.
Strain D's fourth codon becomes GUA, valine instead of glutamic acid.
Strain E gains a codon, AAG, so its polypeptide has an extra lysine.

why.correct: The fourth codon changes from GAA (Glu) to GUA (Val); every other codon is the same. One amino acid replaced by another is a missense mutation, the same kind of change (Glu to Val) as in sickle cell disease.
options: Correct: one codon, one amino acid changed.
GUA codes for valine, not glutamic acid, so the protein does change.
GUA is not a stop codon, so the chain continues.
A base was replaced, not added or removed, so the reading frame is unchanged after it.

why.correct: Deleting U7 shifts the reading frame: AUG GCA GGG AAC UAA… gives Met-Ala-Gly-Asn, then UAA, a stop codon that was not in frame before.
options: Correct: a frameshift changes every codon after it and here reaches a stop early.
This is the normal polypeptide; one deleted base changes the codons after it.
Removing one base does not remove one whole codon; it regroups the rest.
The frame shifts at codon 3, but the stop codon comes two codons later, not at once.

why.correct: Codons are read in threes. Inserting AAG adds one lysine and leaves every later codon in its original frame. Deleting one base regroups all later bases into new codons, which here also creates an early stop.
options: Correct: a multiple of three keeps the frame.
Spliceosomes remove introns, recognized by sequences at their ends; they do not remove inserted bases.
Both insertions and deletions in DNA are copied into the mRNA.
The two changes are close together (positions 7 and 12); position does not explain the difference.

why.correct: Strain C reads AUG (Met), GCA (Ala), then UGA, a stop codon: a nonsense mutation leaves a two-amino-acid chain.

Chemical Q raises revertants from 22 to 380 with or without the extract. Chemical P has no effect alone (24) but raises them to 410 with liver extract, so a product the liver enzymes make from P is the mutagen.
options: Correct: Q acts directly; P must be converted first.
This reverses the two chemicals.
The background of about 22 is the spontaneous rate; the treated plates are 17-19 times higher.
The extract alone gives 25, the same as solvent alone.

why.correct: Spontaneous mutations happen at a low rate in every population: errors that escape proofreading and mismatch repair, and damage from normal chemistry. Among millions of cells, a few happen to restore the gene.
options: Correct: the background is the spontaneous mutation rate.
Nothing suggests the solvent is mutagenic; a spontaneous background is expected.
Mutations are not directed by need; cells cannot choose to change a gene.
The plates are kept sterile and lack histidine for exactly this reason; the counts are steady across plates.

why.correct: The extract alone gives 25 colonies, close to solvent alone (22), so the high counts with chemical P plus extract come from P's product, not from the extract.
options: Correct: a control for the extract.
The plates have no histidine; revertants make their own.
That conclusion needs the chemical P plates; this row only rules out the extract.
Cell numbers were made equal when the plates were spread.

why.correct: A chemical that changes bacterial DNA can change human DNA, and mutations in genes such as tumor suppressors and the genes that drive division can let cells divide out of control (topic 4.6). Such chemicals are carcinogens.
options: Correct: mutagens are likely carcinogens because cancer is caused by mutations.
The histidine gene is just a convenient marker; cancer involves cell-cycle genes.
Bacteria are single cells; they do not get cancer.
The extract only imitates liver chemistry; the link to cancer is through DNA damage.

why.correct: Five of set 1's plates have 0 colonies and two have 64 and 107; set 2's plates all fall in a narrow range around 17.
options: Correct: wide spread in set 1, narrow spread in set 2.
This reverses the two sets.
Set 1 ranges from 0 to 107, far from similar.
Totals are close: 180 in set 1 and 167 in set 2.

why.correct: If contact with phage caused resistance, every plate would show a similar small share, as in set 2. Separate cultures vary hugely because mutations happen at random times during growth: an early one gives a jackpot of resistant offspring, a late one a few, and often none happens at all. Set 2's samples share one history, so they are similar.
options: Correct: random mutations before exposure predict jackpots between independent cultures.
Set 2's steady counts are expected under both hypotheses; set 1's spread is what tells them apart.
Each plate was covered with phage in the same way; only the cultures' separate histories differ.
Resistance came from mutations inside cells; the spread in set 1, not sharing in set 2, is the evidence.

why.correct: 1 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 107 + 0 + 5 + 0 + 64 = 180; 180 ÷ 10 = 18.0. The means of the two sets are similar (18.0 and 16.7); it is the spread that differs.
Samples from one culture differ only by chance in sampling and plating. Their narrow spread shows that technique cannot explain the huge spread among separate cultures.
options: Correct: it is the control for sampling and plating error.
Total resistant cells are similar in both sets, so mutation rate does not differ.
Set 1's cells came from their own separate cultures.
The phage's killing is shown by the few colonies on any plate, not by set 2 specifically.

why.correct: A missense mutation changes one amino acid. The new nonpolar side chain on the outside of the protein makes deoxygenated hemoglobin clump into fibers, which deform red blood cells into sickles that block small vessels and break down early.
options: Correct: one changed side chain, a changed protein shape and interactions, a changed cell.
A base replacement does not shift the reading frame; the chain is full length.
The change is in the coding sequence, and the gene is transcribed normally.
The problem is clumping into fibers at low oxygen, not oxygen being held too tightly.

why.correct: The segment C-D-E has been flipped end to end into E-D-C, with no genes gained or lost: an inversion.
options: Correct: a reversed segment.
A duplication would repeat a segment, such as A-B-C-D-C-D-E-F-G.
A deletion would lose genes, such as A-B-E-F-G.
A translocation moves a segment to a different, nonhomologous chromosome.

why.correct: Transformation, transduction and conjugation are forms of horizontal gene transfer: genes move between cells, not just from parent to offspring.
options: Correct: DNA released by dead cells can be taken up.
Correct: a phage may package host DNA by mistake and deliver it.
Correct: often the DNA moved is a plasmid.
Binary fission passes genes from parent to daughter cells, not between unrelated cells.
Bacteria have no nucleus and do not divide by mitosis.
A spore is the same cell in a resting form; no genes move to another cell.

why.correct: In meiosis I, three homologs cannot split two-and-two; one side gets two and the other one, at random for each chromosome. Almost every gamete ends up with an unbalanced mix and fails, so few seeds form.
options: Correct: odd numbers of sets pair and separate unevenly.
Triploid plants do begin meiosis; the problem is the uneven separation.
The genes are ordinary copies; the problem is the number of sets, not a broken gene.
Many polyploid plants copy their DNA and grow normally; only meiosis fails.

why.correct: Mutations are not directed by need or by the environment. A drug does not create the useful mutation; it removes the cells without one, and the few that already had it multiply.
options: Correct: random mutation, then survival of the cells that happened to carry one.
No signaling system aims mutations at a particular gene; the fluctuation test shows they arise before exposure.
Bacteria mutate; their DNA is copied with errors like any other.
Mutations arise before exposure too, which is what the fluctuation test showed.

why.correct: When two influenza viruses copy their segments in one cell, new particles can package a mix of segments: reassortment. A virus with new combinations of surface proteins can spread in people who have no immunity to it.
options: Correct: reassortment of segments.
Both viruses can copy their segments in the same cell.
Segments stay separate; they are mixed, not fused.
Influenza packages its own RNA segments, not host chromosomes.

why.correct: Transposons are a source of mutations: inserting into a gene usually disrupts it, and the insertion lengthens the DNA where it lands without changing genes elsewhere.

variables.name: Activity of the enzyme the gene codes for
variables.why: Hundreds of extra bases in the coding sequence usually shift the frame or add stop codons, so a working enzyme is rarely made.

variables.name: Length of the DNA of that gene
variables.why: The transposon's DNA is added to the gene.

variables.name: Base sequence of a gene on the other side of the chromosome
variables.why: This insertion changes the gene it lands in, not distant genes.

why.correct: Deleting three bases removes one codon and keeps the frame, so only one amino acid is lost. But that one change disturbs folding; misfolded CFTR is held in the ER and destroyed by the proteasome, so little reaches the membrane.
options: Correct: one missing amino acid, wrong shape, protein destroyed.
Three bases are one codon, so the frame is kept; the stem says the rest of the sequence is normal.
The stem says one amino acid is missing and the rest is normal, so the start is intact.
Protein shape depends on its sequence; one change in a key place can wreck folding.

why.correct: The same allele harms people with two copies, helps carriers survive where malaria is common, and gives no such benefit where malaria is absent. A mutation's effect on survival depends on its environment.
options: Correct: harmful, neutral or helpful depends on context.
Mutations are not directed by the environment; malaria affects who survives, not which mutations occur.
It is common in malaria regions, so it is not harmful in each environment.
Nothing suggests different mutation rates; survival differs, not the rate of mutation.

why.correct: Enzyme E gives one band at 6,000 bp: one cut opens the circle into a single linear piece as long as the plasmid. The other lanes agree: 4,500 + 1,500 = 6,000 and 3,500 + 1,500 + 1,000 = 6,000.
Cutting a circle at n sites gives n pieces. Enzyme B gives two fragments (4,500 and 1,500 bp), so it cuts twice.
options: One cut in a circle gives a single linear piece, as enzyme E shows.
Correct: two cuts in a circle give two pieces.
Three cuts would give three fragments; lane B has two bands.
Four cuts would give four fragments.

why.correct: B sites at 1,000 and 2,500 give B fragments of 1,500 (1,000 to 2,500) and 4,500 (the rest). Adding E's cut at 0 splits the 4,500 piece into 1,000 (0 to 1,000) and 3,500 (2,500 to 6,000): the 3,500, 1,500 and 1,000 bands of the double digest. (The mirror-image map, B sites at 3,500 and 5,000, fits equally well; the gel cannot tell the two directions around the circle apart.)
options: B fragments would be 1,500 and 4,500, but the double digest would give 500, 1,500 and 4,000.
Correct: it reproduces the enzyme B lane and the double digest.
B fragments would be 1,500 and 4,500, but the double digest would give 1,500, 1,500 and 3,000.
B fragments would be 1,500 and 4,500, but the double digest would give 2,000, 1,500 and 2,500.

why.correct: All DNA has about the same charge per base pair, so the pull per unit length is the same. The gel slows long molecules more, so fragments separate by size, small ones farthest.
options: Correct: the gel acts as a sieve.
Charge is proportional to length, so larger fragments carry more charge, not less; the charge per base pair is the same.
All fragments in a lane are loaded together, in one well.
Every base pair has about the same mass, and DNA moves because of charge, not by sinking.

why.correct: The insert is joined into the E site, so the new plasmid has two E sites, one at each end of the insert. Cutting them releases the 900 bp insert and the 6,000 bp plasmid backbone.
options: Correct: cutting at both ends of the insert gives back both pieces.
6,900 bp would be the result of cutting at a single site; this plasmid has two E sites.
The insert would also appear, as a 900 bp band.
Nothing cuts the insert in half unless it has its own E site, which the stem does not say.

why.correct: Sample A's glow is 20.8 at cycle 18 and sample B's is 20.8 at cycle 24.
options: Correct: A crosses six cycles before B.
This swaps the samples; A rises first.
At cycle 20, A is at 57.5 and B at 1.9.
B crosses 20 at about cycle 24 and reaches 100 by cycle 36.

why.correct: A reaches the same glow 24 − 18 = 6 cycles sooner. Each cycle doubles the DNA, so A started with 2<sup>6</sup> = 64 times as much target.
Each cycle uses up primers and nucleotides. Once they run low, and product strands pair with each other instead of with primers, each cycle adds less, and the amount plateaus.
options: Correct: ingredients run out.
The polymerase used in PCR (Taq) is heat-stable, which is why it is used.
Copies have the same length every cycle, set by the two primers.
The dye glows more with double-stranded DNA, which is how the glow tracks product.

why.correct: With every ingredient except template DNA, the glow stays near 1 for 36 cycles. So the rise in the two patient samples needs target DNA from the samples, and the reagents are not contaminated with it.
options: Correct: a negative control.
The flat line shows primers alone do not produce product.
The control contains no patient sample, so it says nothing about the virus in them.
The dye stays near 1 without DNA, so it does not glow on its own.

why.correct: Cells without plasmid cannot grow on ampicillin (plate 2), but 84 colonies grow from the plasmid mixture (plate 4): those cells were transformed, and the plasmid's gene protects them.
options: Correct: transformation plus the protective gene.
The plasmid and cells were mixed before plating; ampicillin only kills cells without the plasmid.
Plate 3 shows most cells did not take it up: the lawn there does not glow.
The drug-survival gene does that; glowing is a separate trait carried on the same plasmid.

why.correct: Transformation is rare. On a plate without ampicillin every cell grows, so the few transformed cells are lost in a lawn of untransformed ones. Ampicillin removes the untransformed cells, which is why the drug-survival gene acts as a selectable marker.
options: Correct: without selection, transformants are a tiny minority.
The glowing colonies on plate 4 show the gene is expressed; nothing suggests ampicillin is needed to switch it on.
Nutrients do not destroy DNA inside cells.
The lawn does not glow because almost none of its cells have the plasmid.

why.correct: 0.10 µg of plasmid was in 1.0 mL; 0.10 mL was spread, so 0.10 × (0.10 ÷ 1.0) = 0.010 µg reached the plate. Efficiency = 84 ÷ 0.010 = 8,400 colonies per µg.

A lawn of untreated cells on plain nutrients confirms the cells survived the treatment and heat shock. Without it, no colonies on plate 2 could mean the cells were dead rather than killed by ampicillin.
options: Correct: a control for cell survival.
Plate 1's cells have no plasmid.
Plate 1 has no plasmid-treated cells; transformants are counted on plate 4.
That is shown by plate 2, compared with plate 1.

why.correct: A restriction enzyme cuts a specific sequence the same way every time, leaving matching single-stranded overhangs. Overhangs from the same enzyme pair with each other, and DNA ligase forms the backbone bonds that make the joint permanent.
options: Correct: complementary overhangs plus ligase.
Restriction enzymes cut; ligase joins.
Ends from different enzymes usually do not match; the same enzyme makes matching ends.
Base pairing between sticky ends is by hydrogen bonds; ligase makes the covalent backbone bonds.

why.correct: Primers can pair only with single strands, so denaturation comes first; the polymerase needs the primers' 3′ ends, so annealing comes before extension; the doubling is the result of the cycle.
Each fragment ends with a chain-stopping nucleotide at the position equal to its length. Reading from length 1 to 8: C (1), A (2), T (3), G (4), C (5), A (6), T (7), G (8): 5′-CATGCATG-3′.
options: Correct: list the bases in order of fragment length.
This is the new strand read from its 3′ end, longest fragment first.
This lists the bases in alphabetical order, not by fragment length.
This swaps the A and T positions.

why.correct: The guide RNA's sequence is complementary to the chosen DNA site, so it leads Cas9 there; Cas9 makes a double-strand break. The cell's quick repair often adds or removes a few bases, which can shift the reading frame and knock out the gene. Supplying a template lets the repair write in a chosen change instead.
options: Correct: base pairing finds the site; Cas9 cuts; repair changes the DNA.
Cas9 cuts DNA, not mRNA, and it finds its target by base pairing, not by reading codons.
The guide RNA is not translated; it works by pairing with DNA.
Standard Cas9 cuts DNA; it does not methylate it.

why.correct: Human genes contain introns. Bacteria have no spliceosomes, so the introns would stay in the mRNA and the protein made from it would be wrong. A DNA copy of the mature mRNA (made with reverse transcriptase) has no introns.
options: Correct: the code is shared, but splicing is not.
The code is shared, but the introns would still be read into the protein.
Bacteria cannot splice; the problem is the introns, not the cap.
Bacteria take up plasmids whatever genes they carry.

why.correct: PCR makes millions of copies of a chosen stretch from a tiny amount of starting DNA, which forensic profiles and virus tests both need.
options: Correct: a few cells' DNA is enough after amplification.
Correct: the viral stretch is copied until it can be detected.
That is gel electrophoresis.
That is done by a restriction enzyme.
That is done by DNA ligase.

why.correct: Each STR site has many possible repeat numbers, and every person carries two (one from each parent). With 13-20 independent sites, the chance two unrelated people match at all of them is tiny.
options: Correct: high variation at many independent sites.
Most STRs used in profiles lie between genes, not in protein-coding sequences.
Everyone has the STR sites; people differ in the number of repeats.
STR lengths are inherited and stay the same in a person's cells.

why.correct: Only changes in germ-line cells, which make gametes, are inherited. Treating bone marrow changes her blood cells, so the benefit is hers alone.
options: Correct: somatic gene therapy is not inherited.
Changes in body (somatic) cells are not passed to offspring.
Blood cells do not transfer their genes into eggs.
Bone marrow stem cells keep dividing, so the change can last for years.
